strengths: Novel and useful theoretical insight: Theorem 1 establishes that DDPO's per-step Gaussian likelihood objective is equivalent (up to Euler-Maruyama discretization error) to denoising score matching conditioned on noisy data, leveraging time-reversal properties of diffusions. This reframing is clean and conceptually clarifying for the field.

Theorem 2 provides a quantitative variance analysis: noisy conditioning strictly inflates the conditional covariance of the DSM target by an explicitly characterized κ(s,t)I, with monotonicity in s. This is a concrete, checkable result rather than a vague claim.

The theory is not left floating: the authors validate the variance prediction with controlled pretraining experiments (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-64) comparing clean vs. noisy DSM under identical settings (Figure 3), directly supporting the mechanism.

Strong empirical results on real text-to-image models (SD3.5M and FLUX) across three reward tasks (GenEval, OCR, PickScore), with large speedups (up to 24×) over Flow-GRPO at matched quality, plus useful ablations (timestep distribution, KL strength, on-policy vs. off-policy).

Practical advantages of decoupling sampling from training (sampler-agnostic, decoupled train/inference timesteps, no CFG in training) are clearly articulated and of independent interest to practitioners.
Reproducibility is supported by pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), hyperparameter details, and stated code release.
weaknesses: The link from the theoretical variance result to RL convergence speed is a heuristic leap. Theorem 2 concerns variance of DSM targets, but in RL post-training the x0 samples come from the evolving policy, and DDPO's per-step formulation offers different credit-assignment properties; the paper does not formally connect variance to the observed speedups, only via analogy to pretraining experiments.

Method novelty is limited. Online reward-weighted denoising/flow-matching fine-tuning has been explored before (Lee et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2025), and the concurrent FMPG (McAllister et al. 2025) uses the ELBO as a policy likelihood. The main original contribution is the DDPO–noisy-DSM equivalence analysis, yet the paper includes no empirical comparison against FMPG or the simplest reward-weighted-ELBO baseline, making it hard to attribute the speedup to the specific insights versus the general approach.

The 'consistent with policy-gradient theory' claim is undermined by the choice of uniform weight w(t)=1, which means the ratio in Equation (11) is no longer an actual likelihood ratio of the policy—the objective becomes a heuristic advantage-weighted loss rather than an unbiased policy gradient. The paper acknowledges likelihood/visual-quality mismatch but does not discuss the resulting bias in the gradient estimate.

Evaluation is reward-only: GenEval, OCR, and PickScore measure the finetuning reward itself. There are no metrics of general generation quality (e.g., FID, diversity), so potential reward hacking or quality degradation—explicitly a known risk for such methods—is not assessed. The comparison also stops at 'matching' Flow-GRPO rather than exceeding it, and the reported speedups depend on the (unstated in detail) definition of convergence.
Baselines are narrow: only Flow-GRPO is compared, despite the existence of DanceGRPO, MixGRPO, BranchGRPO, ReFL/DRaFT, etc., which would better contextualize the speedup claims.

No explicit limitations section; the code URL in the abstract is empty; minor presentation issues exist (broken formatting in Lemma 1, garbled notation in Figure 1a, 'max log p(x0|xt)+A(x0)' is not a well-defined objective as written).
Scope is confined to two image models and three reward tasks; claims of generality (e.g., video, other modalities) remain untested.

strengths: The paper asks a well-motivated and conceptually interesting question: why do diffusion RL post-training objectives (DDPO-style per-step Gaussian likelihoods) differ from the score/flow matching objectives used in pretraining, and what does the DDPO loss actually optimize?

The theoretical analysis (Theorems 1-2, Lemma 1) is coherent and cleanly presented: the DDPO-step = noisy-DSM equivalence via time reversal of diffusions (Haussmann-Pardoux), and the quantitative variance inflation kappa(s,t) with monotonicity in conditioning noise level s, are nice, checkable results.

The CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64 controlled pretraining experiments (Figure 3) provide a sensible validation of the variance claim by directly comparing clean- vs noisy-conditioned DSM under identical settings.

The AWM algorithm is simple, sampler-agnostic, and decouples training timesteps from sampling, which is practically attractive. Empirical coverage is reasonably broad (SD3.5M and FLUX, three reward tasks) with substantial reported wall-clock speedups over Flow-GRPO.
Ablations (timestep distribution, KL strength beta, on-policy vs. mixed off-policy) are relevant and reported against wall-clock time rather than iteration count, which is the right axis.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the method: advantage/reward-weighted score matching is essentially reward-weighted regression for diffusion (Lee et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2025), which the paper itself acknowledges in Sec. 2.1.3. The concurrent FMPG (McAllister et al. 2025) already proposes ELBO-based policy likelihood. Crucially, no empirical comparison against a plain reward-weighted score-matching baseline is provided, so it is unclear what the theoretical framing adds beyond these prior methods in practice.

The claimed equivalence between DDPO and noisy-DSM 'omits the discretization error induced by Euler-Maruyama discretization' — but in practice DDPO/Flow-GRPO use a small fixed number of steps (tens), so the omitted error is not obviously negligible. The paper does not quantify this gap, weakening the central theoretical claim's applicability to the methods it critiques.

Conceptually, redefining the MDP so that the entire trajectory is a single action pi(a|s)=p(x0|c) reduces RL to weighted maximum likelihood and discards trajectory-level credit assignment; the substitution of the ELBO for the exact likelihood inside the importance ratio in Eq. (11) introduces an unquantified bias that is not analyzed. Claims that AWM is 'consistent with policy-gradient theory' are thus overstated.

Evaluation relies entirely on the training rewards themselves (GenEval, OCR accuracy, PickScore) as the evaluation metrics. This raises a serious reward-hacking confound: faster reward increase may reflect exploitation of the reward models rather than genuine quality gains. No side metrics (e.g., FID on fixed prompts, HPS, diversity/precision-recall, human evaluation) or inspection for degeneration are reported. PickScore improvements are marginal (23.02 vs 23.01) yet headline speedups are derived from such near-ties.

Reproducibility is undermined: the code availability URL is literally blank in the manuscript ('Code is available at .'). No seeds, error bars, or variance across runs are reported for any headline result, despite inherently stochastic RL training.

There is no limitations section and no discussion of failure modes (e.g., reward over-optimization, mode collapse from amplifying high-reward samples, behavior when advantages are mostly negative), which the method's variance-benefit narrative makes especially relevant.

Presentation inconsistencies: the abstract claims 'up to 24x speedup' while Figure 1c and the GenEval result report 8.02x; Figure 5 caption vs. Table 2 numbers require cross-referencing to reconcile; several typos (e.g., 'AWM is implicit doing denoising score matching'). Figure 5a shows a '23.5x speedup' annotation that matches only the single OCR task on SD3.5M, and the model may have 'not compromising generation quality' is asserted but only supported by cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figure 6).

The baseline comparison is restricted to Flow-GRPO; DanceGRPO, TempFlow-GRPO, MixGRPO, and ReFL/DRaFT-style methods are discussed in related work but not compared, so the efficiency claims are against a single baseline.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and interesting theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 shows that DDPO's per-step likelihood maximization is (up to Euler–Maruyama discretization error) equivalent to denoising score matching with noisy conditioning, and Theorem 2 quantifies the extra variance induced by noisy conditioning via an explicit, monotone term κ(s,t). The proofs (Appendix B) are reasonably complete and build cleanly on time-reversal of diffusions (Haussmann & Pardoux).

The theoretical claims are empirically corroborated with controlled pretraining experiments (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-64) comparing clean-DSM vs. noisy-DSM objectives under identical settings, directly supporting the variance analysis.

The proposed method (AWM) is simple, well-motivated by the theory, and delivers substantial and consistent efficiency gains: matching Flow-GRPO's GenEval score (0.95) with ~8× fewer GPU hours, ~23.6× on OCR (SD3.5M), and gains across FLUX on OCR and PickScore.

Useful ablations are provided on timestep sampling distributions, KL regularization strength β, and on-policy vs. one-step off-policy updates, giving practical guidance (e.g., instability at β=0.2, degradation with logit-normal timesteps).
The method's decoupling of sampling and training (any sampler, decoupled train/sample timesteps) is a genuine practical advantage over DDPO-style methods tied to Euler–Maruyama discretization.
Related work coverage is thorough, including concurrent approaches (FMPG, reward-weighted regression lines), and the positioning against ReFL/DDPO/RWR families is clear.
weaknesses: A gap between theory and method: the policy-gradient justification relies on using the ELBO as a surrogate for sequence log-likelihood, but the practice uses uniform time weighting w(t)=1, which is explicitly stated to work better — this departs from the ELBO/policy-gradient interpretation the paper claims. The bias introduced by replacing exact likelihood with a weighted score-matching surrogate is never quantified, weakening the claim that AWM is 'consistent with policy-gradient theory'.

The importance ratio in Equation (11) (exp of a difference of score-matching losses with shared timesteps/noise) is a heuristic surrogate for the true likelihood ratio; its bias and variance relative to the actual πθ/πθold ratio are not analyzed, so the GRPO framing is largely conceptual rather than exact.

The variance analysis is validated only via proxy pretraining experiments (noisy-DSM vs. clean-DSM on CIFAR-10/ImageNet-64), not by an actual small-scale DDPO vs. AWM RL comparison, leaving a chain of inference between Theorem 2 and the claimed cause of DDPO's slow RL convergence.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on reward metrics (GenEval, OCR accuracy, PickScore). The claim of 'without compromising generation quality' is under-supported: no FID, no diversity/precision-recall measures after RL, and only qualitative image comparisons. Since negative advantages actively push the velocity away from targets, quality/diversity degradation is a plausible risk that is not measured.

Baselines are limited to Flow-GRPO. No comparison against DanceGRPO, TempFlow-GRPO, MixGRPO, or BranchGRPO, several of which also target efficiency; the reported speedups may partly reflect a suboptimally configured baseline rather than an inherent advantage of AWM.

Statistical rigor is missing: no multiple seeds, error bars, or variance reporting on any of the headline speedup numbers; convergence-criterion-based speedups (e.g., 24×) can be sensitive to where curves are read off.

Reproducibility gaps: the code link in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at .'), training prompt sets, batch sizes, and evaluation protocols for the RL runs are underspecified, and the sampler/timestep details needed to reproduce the exact speedup figures are incomplete.

There is no limitations section. Notable limitations — the discretization-error caveat in Theorem 1, the ad-hoc uniform time weighting, absence of exact-likelihood evaluation, and reliance on a single baseline — should be acknowledged by the authors.

Some of the theoretical content is incremental: Lemma 1 is a direct generalization of Vincent (2011), and the DDPO–DSM equivalence follows fairly directly from time-reversal; the novelty lies mainly in assembling these into a variance narrative and a practical method.

strengths: Clear and interesting conceptual contribution: the paper establishes, via time-reversal arguments (Haussmann–Pardoux), that the DDPO per-step reverse-transition likelihood induces a population objective equivalent to denoising score matching with a noisy target, and that the advantage-weighted DDPO gradient locally equals an advantage-weighted clean-target DSM gradient (Theorem 2.1 + Lemma 2.2 + Eq. 10). This unifies diffusion RL post-training with the pretraining objective in a conceptually satisfying way, mirroring the LLM pretrain/RL alignment story.

The variance analysis (Theorem 2.3, with explicit covariance inflation kappa(s,t) and its monotonicity) is concrete and predictive, and the authors empirically validate it both directly (target-variance measurements in Table 6) and behaviorally (noisy-target DSM pretraining converges more slowly on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64 in Figure 3). This theory-to-practice loop strengthens the paper.

Strong empirical results: substantial speedups over Flow-GRPO on two modern backbones (SD3.5M, FLUX) across three reward families (GenEval, OCR, PickScore, plus ImageReward in the appendix), with equal or better final quality (e.g., GenEval 0.985 vs 0.95; OCR 0.92 in 21.76 vs 415.9 GPU hours). Decoupling training from sampling is a practically valuable design that also enables arbitrary samplers.

Reasonably thorough ablations (Monte Carlo steps, EMA rollout with IS correction, KL coefficient, ODE vs SDE samplers), honest reporting of earlier configurations in the appendix, diversity preservation shown after 600 RL steps, and a clear algorithm/pipeline description that supports reproducibility.

Writing and figure design are clear; the related-work section carefully distinguishes AWM from RWR/AWR-style reward-weighted regression (signed policy-gradient weights vs. nonnegative exponential weights) and from concurrent ELBO-likelihood approaches (FMPG).
weaknesses: The central equivalence (Theorem 2.1) is population-level and explicitly ignores the Euler–Maruyama discretization bias that real DDPO incurs; this gap is acknowledged but never quantified, so the claim 'DDPO is secretly doing noisy DSM' is exact only in an idealized setting.

Lemma 2.2 is a direct generalization of the classical Vincent (2011) result, and the variance argument follows known control-variate reasoning; the theory is clean but individually incremental. Lemma 2.2 also links objectives with the same population minimizer under expectation, which does not by itself establish that per-sample gradients or optimization dynamics are equivalent.

The off-policy machinery relies on a heuristic 'likelihood ratio' exp(-(l_theta - l_ref)) built from an ELBO/Monte-Carlo surrogate (Eq. 15), which is not an exact density ratio; the EMA+IS ablation shows this variant is only competitive (not better) than the on-policy version, and the theoretical justification for using the ELBO surrogate as an importance-sampling ratio is underdeveloped.

Speedup comparisons may be partly confounded by engineering choices beyond the core objective: AWM uses a different sampler (SA-Solver), reduced training timesteps, cfg=1.0 vs. Flow-GRPO's settings, and on-policy single-update batches; while the paper argues these are benefits of the design, the headline 16–34x numbers are not decomposed into objective-level vs. sampler/schedule-level gains. Comparisons to other recent baselines (DanceGRPO, MixGRPO, BranchGRPO) are discussed but not empirically run except TempFlow-GRPO on GenEval.

Evaluation is limited to text-to-image reward benchmarks (GenEval, OCR, PickScore, ImageReward) with known saturation/reward-hacking concerns; no human evaluation or study on the method's behavior with denser/process rewards or outside image domains, and no evidence on potential negative-advantage 'push-away' degradation modes.

Several experimental details appear only in the appendix (e.g., the two-phase on/off-policy setup in the early configuration, choice of w(t)=1 vs w(t)=t) and the configuration changed mid-project; while honestly reported, this complicates exact reproduction of the headline numbers.

strengths: The central theoretical insight is interesting and clearly communicated: Theorem 2.1 shows the DDPO per-step likelihood induces a noisy-target denoising score matching objective, Lemma 2.2 bridges noisy- and clean-target DSM, and Theorem 2.3 quantifies the excess conditional covariance κ(s,t) with a clean monotonicity statement. The theory is validated empirically both by pretraining experiments (Figure 3) and direct target-variance measurements (Table 6).

The proposed method (AWM) is simple, well-motivated by the theory, and practical: it reuses the pretrained flow-matching loss with advantage weights, decouples sampling from training (allowing any sampler), and avoids per-step likelihood computation. Algorithm 1 and the pipeline figure make the method easy to reproduce.

Experiments cover two strong modern backbones (SD3.5M, FLUX) and three reward types (GenEval, OCR, PickScore, plus ImageReward in the appendix), with ablations over Monte Carlo steps, rollout model, KL coefficient, and ODE vs SDE sampling. Mode-collapse is checked qualitatively (Figure 10).

The related-work discussion is unusually thorough, including an explicit and honest positioning against reward-weighted regression (RWR/AWR, Lee et al. 2023, Fan et al. 2025) and the concurrent FMPG, with a clear articulation of the signed-weight distinction.
The appendix discloses LLM usage and provides both early and final experimental configurations, which supports some degree of reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: advantage/reward-weighted denoising-loss fine-tuning already exists (Lee et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2025; concurrent FMPG). The genuinely new elements are the DDPO≡noisy-DSM analysis and the signed (policy-gradient) weighting, which is a relatively incremental delta over prior weighted-regression approaches.

The headline 'up to 34× speedup' claims rest on a weak evaluation protocol: speed-up is measured as GPU hours to reach a threshold metric, comparing against a single baseline (Flow-GRPO). Hyperparameters, samplers, and weighting schemes differ substantially between AWM and Flow-GRPO (Section F.1 vs F.2), and the appendix shows the measured speed-up swings from 8.02× to 16.54× purely with configuration changes, so the headline number appears highly sensitive to tuning and the baseline fairness is unclear.

Several comparisons undercut the headline claims: in Table 2, the AWM† variant for SD3.5M PickScore requires MORE GPU hours (992.0 vs 956.1) for a +0.43% gain; GenEval is nearly saturated (0.985–0.99), making differences hard to interpret; and no comparison is made against other strong recent baselines (e.g., DanceGRPO) beyond the summary row for TempFlow-GRPO.

The theory is confined to an idealized setting: population-level objectives, oracle single-step analysis, omission of Euler–Maruyama discretization bias, and a linear (Gaussian/VP) forward process. The full advantage-weighted connection (Section C.3) is only a local-gradient statement at a frozen rollout policy, so the gap between the analyzed objective and the actually optimized GRPO surrogate (with ratios, KL, clipping omitted) is not fully closed.

The KL term is estimated via a velocity-space proxy (Eq. 16) and the policy likelihood via an ELBO surrogate (Eq. 14–15) whose gap to the true likelihood is not controlled in the RL setting; the impact of these approximations on correctness of the derived policy gradient is not analyzed.

Statistical rigor is thin: no error bars, seeds, or variance estimates for benchmark scores; sample diversity is argued only from a handful of qualitative images; and reward-hacking behavior (a known risk with these objectives) is not studied beyond the KL ablation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link in the abstract is empty ('available at'), and the two configurations described in the appendix make it difficult to know exactly which recipe produced the main-paper numbers.

Limitations are only briefly addressed (mainly in the impact statement); there is no dedicated discussion of failure modes, benchmark saturation, or the applicability of the idealized theory to practice.

strengths: Clear and insightful theoretical contribution: the paper proves (Theorem 2.1 + Lemma 2.2) that the DDPO per-step likelihood, viewed at the population level via the forward–reverse joint distribution identity (Haussmann–Pardoux), is secretly denoising score matching with a noisy target that shares the same population minimizer as clean-target DSM. This cleanly explains why DDPO-style RL diverges from the pretraining objective and is a genuinely useful conceptual reframing.

The variance analysis (Theorem 2.3) is quantitative rather than hand-wavy: it derives an explicit closed-form covariance inflation κ(s,t) for noisy-target vs. clean-target DSM, proves strict monotonicity in s, and validates the prediction both with direct variance measurements (Table 6) and pretraining FID experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64 (Figure 3). This tight theory–experiment loop strengthens the central claim.

The proposed method (AWM) follows directly and logically from the analysis: keep the pretraining score/flow-matching loss and reweight per-sample by advantage. The policy-gradient derivation (Section 3, Eq. 13–17) is coherent, and the signed weighting is clearly differentiated from reward-weighted regression in Appendix E.3.

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent speedups (16.54× on GenEval, 19.13×/34.67× on OCR/PickScore for SD3.5M; 8.53×/6.82× on FLUX) across three reward types and two modern backbones, with ablations on Monte Carlo steps, rollout model (on-policy vs. EMA+IS), KL coefficient, and sampler compatibility (ODE vs. SDE, Figure 8).

Good transparency and reproducibility practices: full pseudocode, hyperparameter details for both early and final configurations, honest reporting of earlier-experiment results in Tables 4–5/Figure 9, and a stated code release.
A brief but appropriate impact statement acknowledging potential misuse.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to verifier/reward-model-based metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore, ImageReward). The claim of 'without compromising generation quality' is supported mainly by a qualitative diversity figure (Figure 10) rather than standard distributional quality metrics (e.g., FID on a benchmark, CLIP-based checks for prompt fidelity collapse), so the no-degradation claim is only weakly substantiated.

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparisons are almost exclusively against Flow-GRPO (plus TempFlow-GRPO on GenEval). Other RL post-training baselines (DDPO, DPOK, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL/DRAFT-style methods) are discussed but not empirically compared on SD3.5M/FLUX, making it hard to situate the gains.

Speed-up figures are defined at matched metric levels and rely on single training runs without seeds or error bars; given the noisy reward curves (e.g., FLUX PickScore in Figure 5d), variance in the reported speedups is a concern. Additionally, AWM's final full-training scores are sometimes only marginally higher than Flow-GRPO's, so the headline contribution is efficiency rather than quality.

The theory is an idealized, single-step, population-level analysis that explicitly omits Euler–Maruyama discretization error and applies at a frozen rollout policy; the connection between this idealized equivalence and actual finite-step, finite-batch RL dynamics is asserted rather than quantified.

The KL penalty is implemented as an ELBO/velocity-space surrogate (Eq. 15–16) rather than an exact likelihood ratio; combined with negative-advantage samples actively pushing away from targets, this introduces reward-hacking risk that is not empirically probed (e.g., no adversarial prompt or degradation study), even though the paper itself lists reward hacking as a motivation for regularization.

Novelty of the core method is incremental relative to concurrent and prior reward-weighted flow-matching work (Lee et al. 2023, Fan et al. 2025, concurrent FMPG, FwmPG); the paper's differentiation rests mainly on the noisy-DSM analysis and the policy-gradient derivation, which is a fair but not overwhelming distinction.

Missing or thin treatment of some limitations in the main text: dependence of results on specific reward functions, the linear-Gaussian assumption underlying Theorem 2.3, and the gap between GenEval-style saturation (near-1.0 scores) and meaningful capability differences.
